The publication explicitly notes that when school principal responses are presented, they are weighted to be proportionate to the number of 15-year-olds enrolled in the school, indicating the use of complex survey weighting at least for school-level reporting. For student-level results and trend comparisons, the report discusses the use of sampling weights and adjustments for comparability over time (e.g., Austria 2000 weight adjustments; Israel 2000 adjustments for gender composition), and it also describes that PISA uses multilevel modelling with weights at both student and school levels (updated since 2000). sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The report uses the PISA 2009 target population of 15-year-olds (aged 15 years 3 months to 16 years 2 months) who have completed at least 6 years of formal schooling, regardless of institution type. For trend analyses, it applies additional comparability filters: reading trends are computed only for countries with valid results in both PISA 2000 and PISA 2009 (38 countries), mathematics trends for countries with valid results in both PISA 2003 and PISA 2009 (39 countries), and science trends for countries with valid results in both PISA 2006 and PISA 2009 (56 countries). It also excludes countries from specific comparisons when methodological or administration issues invalidate comparability (e.g., Austria excluded from trend comparisons due to boycott and removal of identifiable cases; Netherlands/UK excluded for specific 2000 comparisons due to response-rate or methodological problems). For equity analyses involving immigrant status and home language, it further restricts to countries meeting minimum sample requirements (at least 30 students with the relevant subgroup across at least five schools).

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA 2009 volume reports learning trends in reading (2000–2009), and shorter-span trend updates in mathematics (2003–2009) and science (2006–2009). The assessment covers about 470,000 students in 2009 across 65 participating countries and economies, with each student completing two hours of pencil-and-paper tasks in reading, mathematics and science, plus a 30-minute student questionnaire and a school principal questionnaire. In a subset of 20 countries, additional computer-based questions were administered to assess reading digital texts. Trend estimation relies on comparability procedures across cycles, including common items and scale equating, and it applies statistical significance criteria and p-value reporting based on replications. The report also adjusts trend estimates for demographic and socio-economic composition changes (e.g., age/gender, ESCS, immigrant background, and home language) and discusses how methodological issues (response rates, administration changes, and dataset exclusions) affect which countries can be compared over time. Overall, it documents substantial cross-country variation in mean performance changes and in equity-related indicators such as proficiency-level distributions and socio-economic gradients.
